Return only JSON {"skills":[{"category":"general or one supplied official category","trigger":"when to apply","steps":["concrete image check","how to distinguish alternatives"]}]}. No case/patient ID, option letter, figure number, patient-specific number, copied question, or rule merely repeating the reference diagnosis. General medical findings are allowed. A 56-year-old female with a history of heavy smoking and previous chickenpox infection presents with cough and dyspnea. A chest radiograph (Fig. 1) reveals multiple small nodular opacities with random distribution, some of which are dense, suggesting calcification, and a spiculated nodule in the right perihilar region. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis based solely on the chest X-ray findings, and what is the rationale for this diagnosis?

A) Metastatic pulmonary calcification; because of the presence of calcified nodules and the patient's smoking history.
B) Healed varicella zoster virus pneumonia; due to the presence of calcified nodules and a history of chickenpox.
C) Pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis; given the calcified nodules and random distribution.
D) Tuberculosis; suggested by the spiculated nodule and calcified nodules.
E) Undifferentiated adenocarcinoma; indicated by the spiculated nodule in the right perihilar region.
F) Pneumoconiosis; based on the random distribution of nodular opacities and calcification.
